summary: This document defines how to run Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) on Link Aggregation Group (LAG) interfaces. It runs an independent Asynchronous mode BFD session on every LAG member link, so each member link can be checked for continuity.

plainLanguage.summary: Several cables are bundled together and presented to the network as one link, so that the network keeps working when one cable fails. Finding out which cable has failed is usually left to the protocol that manages the bundle. This RFC adds a second way to find out: a small liveness check, called BFD, running separately on every cable in the bundle. Each check is independent, and a cable is taken out of use as soon as its check fails.

questions: how to detect failed lag member links
what udp port does micro-bfd use
how does bfd detect lag member link failure
subtitle: Run a separate BFD session on every cable in a link bundle, so a failed member is noticed quickly and pulled out of use.

tldr.problem: A link aggregation group combines several physical links into one logical link, so a single failed cable is normally hidden from the rest of the network. The Link Aggregation Control Protocol can detect a failed member, but it is slower, and a bundle configured without it has no member-level detection at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC runs an independent Asynchronous mode BFD session on every member link, one for each address family in use, each with its own discriminators and its own state machine. The sessions use a dedicated UDP destination port, 6784, and on Ethernet member links a dedicated multicast MAC address.
tldr.outcome: A dead member link is noticed within the BFD detection time and removed from the load-balancing table, so the rest of the bundle keeps working. The load balancer also refuses to use a member link until its sessions are up, which closes a blind spot for the layer 3 protocols that see only the bundle.

today: RFC 7130 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. IANA has assigned the dedicated MAC address 01-00-5E-90-00-01 and the UDP port 6784 for BFD on link aggregation group interfaces, and both registry entries now point at this document.

sections.title: Why Check Every Member Link
sections.content:
The Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol of RFC 5880 provides a mechanism to detect faults in the bidirectional path between two forwarding engines, including interfaces, data links and, to the extent possible, the forwarding engines themselves, with potentially very low latency. BFD also provides a fast mechanism for detecting communication failures on any data links, and the protocol can run over any media and at any protocol layer.

LAG, as defined in IEEE 802.1AX, provides mechanisms to combine multiple physical links into a single logical link. The logical link gives higher bandwidth and better resiliency, because if one of the physical member links fails, the aggregate logical link can continue to forward traffic over the remaining operational member links.

Currently the Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) is used to detect failures on a per-physical-member basis. Using BFD for failure detection would give faster detection, would give detection in the absence of LACP, and would be able to verify the ability of each member link to forward layer 3 packets. Running a single BFD session over the aggregation, without internal knowledge of the member links, would make it impossible for BFD to guarantee detection of the physical member link failures.

The goal is therefore to verify link continuity for every member link, which corresponds to Section 7.3 of RFC 5882. The approach is to run an Asynchronous mode BFD session over each LAG member link, and to make BFD control whether the member link should be part of the layer 2 load-balancing table of the LAG interface, whether or not LACP is in use. The document describes how to establish an Asynchronous mode BFD session per physical LAG member link of the LAG interface.

There are native Ethernet mechanisms for detecting failures, 802.1ax and 802.3ah, that could be used for LAG, but the solution defined here enables operators who have already deployed BFD over other technologies, such as IP or MPLS, to use a common failure detection mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage:
BFD is a liveness check between two routers. Each side sends small packets at a fixed rate, and if the other side stops answering, the path is declared broken, usually much faster than the routing protocol would notice.

On a bundle of cables, one BFD session for the whole bundle would only tell you that the bundle is broken. Running a separate session on each cable tells you which cable is broken, so the bundle can keep running on the others. The check also works when the bundle is not managed by the link aggregation protocol at all.

sections.title: Micro-BFD Sessions on Every Member Link
sections.content:
The mechanism defined for fast detection of a LAG member link failure is to run Asynchronous mode BFD sessions on every LAG member link. The document calls these per-member-link BFD sessions micro-BFD sessions.

Member link micro-BFD sessions, when using IP/UDP encapsulation, can use IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. Two micro-BFD sessions MAY exist per member link, one for each address family. When an address family is used on one member link, then it MUST be used on all member links of that LAG.

A single micro-BFD session for every enabled address family runs on each member link of the LAG, and the negotiation of each session MUST follow the same procedures as in RFC 5880 and RFC 5881. Only Asynchronous mode BFD is considered; the BFD echo function is out of scope. At least one system MUST take the Active role, possibly both.

The micro-BFD sessions on the member links are independent BFD sessions. They use their own unique local discriminator values, maintain their own set of state variables, and have their own independent state machines. Timer values MAY differ between them, even among sessions belonging to the same aggregation, although it is expected that sessions belonging to the same aggregation will use the same timer values.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each cable in the bundle gets its own BFD session, and each session is a complete session of its own: its own identifier, its own state, its own timers. Two sessions may exist on one cable, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6, but if a bundle uses an address family on one cable it has to use it on all of them.

Only the plain Asynchronous mode is used here. The echo function, where a packet is sent back to its own sender, is not covered.

sections.title: Telling the Sessions Apart
sections.content:
The demultiplexing of a received BFD packet is based solely on the Your Discriminator field when that field is nonzero. For the initial Down BFD packets of a session, this value MAY be zero, and in that case demultiplexing MUST be based on some combination of other fields that MUST include the interface information of the member link and the destination UDP port of the received packet.

The reception procedure of Section 6.8.6 of RFC 5880 is amended for micro-BFD sessions: if the Your Discriminator field is nonzero and a micro-BFD session is found, the interface on which the BFD control packet arrived MUST correspond to the interface associated with that session. Without that rule, a packet arriving on one member link could be answered by the session belonging to another.

The BFD control packets for each micro-BFD session are IP/UDP encapsulated as defined in RFC 5881, but with a new UDP destination port, 6784. The new port removes the ambiguity between BFD over LAG packets and BFD over single-hop IP, which would otherwise arise, for example, from configuring a LAG with micro-BFD sessions on one side and a RFC 5881 BFD session for the LAG as a single interface on the other side. The procedures in this document MUST be used for BFD messages addressed to port 6784 and MUST NOT be used for other ports assigned to other BFD modes.

Control packets use a destination IP address that is configured on the peer system and can be reached through the LAG interface. Implementations may range from explicitly configuring IP addresses for the BFD sessions to out-of-band methods for learning the destination IP address; the details are outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each session is normally matched to its packets by the identifier the far end puts in every packet. The very first packets of a session, sent before the far end knows the identifier, carry no identifier, so they are matched by the cable they arrived on and the port number they were sent to.

All these sessions use one port of their own, 6784, so that a micro-BFD packet cannot be mistaken for an ordinary single-hop BFD packet. That matters when one end of a bundle is configured the two different ways.

sections.title: Details on Ethernet Member Links
sections.content:
On Ethernet-based LAG member links, the destination Media Access Control (MAC) address is the dedicated multicast MAC address 01-00-5E-90-00-01, which is to be the immediate next hop. This dedicated MAC address MUST be used for the initial BFD packets of a micro-BFD session when it is in the Down, AdminDown and Init states. When a micro-BFD session is changing into the Up state, the first bfd.DetectMult packets in the Up state MUST be sent with the dedicated MAC. For BFD packets in the Up state following the first bfd.DetectMult packets, the source MAC address from the received BFD packets for the session MAY be used instead of the dedicated MAC.

All implementations MUST be able to send and receive BFD packets in the Up state using the dedicated MAC address. Implementations that support sending Up packets with both the dedicated and the received MAC address need to offer means to control the behaviour. On Ethernet-based LAG member links, the source MAC SHOULD be the MAC address of the member link transmitting the packet. The dedicated address helps to reduce the number of additional MAC addresses, which reduces the resources needed on the Ethernet hardware of the receiving member link.

Micro-BFD packets SHOULD always be sent untagged. When the LAG operates in the context of IEEE 802.1q or IEEE 802.qinq, the micro-BFD packets may either be untagged or sent with a VLAN tag of Zero, that is 802.1p priority tagged. Implementations compliant with this standard MUST be able to receive both untagged and 802.1p priority tagged micro-BFD packets.
sections.plainLanguage:
On a bundle of Ethernet cables, the packets are addressed to one multicast MAC address reserved for this purpose, so that every member link can be addressed with the same destination address without needing an address of its own. That saves resources on the receiving hardware.

The packets are normally sent without a VLAN tag. Inside a tagged network they may be sent with a tag of zero, which marks the priority but not the network, and any implementation has to be able to receive both forms.

sections.title: How BFD and the Bundle Interact
sections.content:
The micro-BFD sessions for a particular LAG member link MUST be requested when the member link state is either Distributing or Standby, and the sessions MUST be deleted when the member link is in neither of those states any more.

BFD is used to control whether the load-balancing algorithm is able to select a particular LAG member link. In other words, even when LACP is used and considers the member link ready to forward traffic, the member link MUST NOT be used by the load balancer until all the micro-BFD sessions of that member link are in the Up state.

Where an implementation has separate load-balancing tables for IPv4 and IPv6, and both an IPv4 and an IPv6 micro-BFD session exist for a member link, the implementation MAY enable the member link in the load-balancing algorithm based on the BFD session with the matching address family alone.

There is one exception, for the BFD packets themselves. Implementations MAY receive and transmit BFD packets through the Aggregator's MAC service interface, independently of the session state.
sections.plainLanguage:
A member link's BFD sessions exist only while that link is one of the ones the bundle is using. The rule that matters is the second one: the load balancer must leave a member link out of its table until that link's BFD session has come up, even if the link aggregation protocol considers the link ready.

The BFD packets themselves are exempt, so that a session can start and finish even when the link is not yet carrying traffic.

sections.title: BFD on Member Links and Layer 3 Protocols
sections.content:
The mechanism described in the document is likely to be used by modules that manage interfaces or LAGs, and so manage the member links of a LAG. Typical layer 3 protocols such as OSPF have no insight into the LAG and treat it as one bigger interface. The signalling from the micro sessions to the layer 3 protocols is therefore done indirectly, through the effect of the micro-BFD sessions on the load-balancing table and through the interface and LAG managing module's potential decision to shut down the LAG.

An active method of testing the impact of the micro-BFD sessions is for the layer 3 protocols to request a single BFD session per LAG.
sections.plainLanguage:
The routing protocols above the bundle do not know that the bundle is made of several cables. They see one interface. So the information from the per-cable checks reaches them indirectly: a cable that fails is taken out of the load-balancing table, and the module that manages the bundle may decide to shut the whole bundle down.

A way to check that this indirect signalling works is to ask the routing protocol for one ordinary BFD session on the bundle as a whole.

sections.title: Detecting a Member Link Failure
sections.content:
When a micro-BFD session goes down, that member link MUST be taken out of the LAG load-balancing table.

Where an implementation has separate load-balancing tables for IPv4 and IPv6, and both an IPv4 and an IPv6 micro-BFD session exist for a member link, the implementation MAY remove the member link only from the load-balancing table that matches the address family of the failing BFD session. For example, if the IPv4 micro-BFD session fails but the IPv6 micro-BFD session stays Up, the member link MAY be removed from only the IPv4 load balancing table, and the link MAY remain in the IPv6 load-balancing table. Alternatively, the member link may be removed from both tables. This decision is an implementation detail.

The appendix of the document adds further operational detail. If the feature were provisioned on an aggregated link member after the link was already active within a LAG, the BFD session state should not influence the load-balancing algorithm until the session reaches the Up state, so that enabling the LAG and enabling BFD on it has no impact on the forwarding service. If the feature were deprovisioned while the session was in the Up state, BFD should move to the AdminDown state and attempt to tell the peer. If the local or the remote state of a session is AdminDown, the system should not indicate a connectivity failure to any client and should not remove the member link from forwarding, and this is independent of the use of LACP.

Where traffic is forwarded across a link while the corresponding micro-BFD session is not in the Up state, an implementation may use a configurable timeout after which the session must have reached the Up state, otherwise the link is taken out of forwarding, and the configuration must allow that timeout to be turned off. The timeout ensures that a LAG does not stay for ever in an inconsistent state where forwarding occurs on a link with no confirmation from the micro-BFD session that the link is healthy.

The appendix ends with a warning about a mismatch: if one device is not operating a micro-BFD session on a link while the other is, and the second perceives the session to be Down, the two devices have a different view of the status of the link, which would likely lead to traffic loss across the LAG. Another protocol can be used to bootstrap BFD to detect such a mismatched configuration, since the side that is not configured can send a rejection error, but such bootstrapping mechanisms are outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage:
When a session fails, the cable comes out of the load-balancing table at once. If a bundle keeps separate tables for the two address families, a cable may be removed from one table and kept in the other, or removed from both; that is an implementation choice.

Two operational cautions are given. A session that is deliberately shut down, on either end, should not be treated as a failure, and should not take the cable out of use. And if the two ends are configured differently, one running the session and the other not, they will disagree about the state of the cable, which is likely to cost traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no additional security issues, and the security mechanisms defined in RFC 5880 apply to it.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no security rules of its own: the security mechanisms that BFD already defines apply here unchanged.

items.title: UDP destination port
items.text: 6784, so that these packets cannot be confused with single-hop BFD.

items.title: Destination MAC address
items.text: The dedicated multicast address 01-00-5E-90-00-01 on Ethernet member links.

items.title: Tagging
items.text: Sent untagged, or with a VLAN tag of zero where the bundle is tagged.

items.title: Interface check
items.text: A packet must arrive on the member link that the session belongs to.
